Her cousin Imran, sewing buttons at the next machine, looked up. "The fifteenth is the date. Why the tenth?"

"I'm finishing on the 10th," she said.
"The deadline is the 15th."
"I know. But last term the school printer broke the week everything was due, and half my class handed in late. And in April I had the flu for five days." She drew a box around the 10th. "So those five days are for whatever goes wrong."

I'm Jaya, and in my first year of college I learned something about money the hard way.
Papa sent my allowance on the first of each month, and by the twentieth it was always gone. Then in October my laptop charger died two days after the allowance came. A new one took a big chunk, and I spent the rest of the month borrowing from my friend Jatin and skipping canteen lunches. I felt so embarrassed asking again and again.
In November I did something different. On the day the money came, I took out a small amount and put it in a separate pouch in my cupboard. I called it the "things break" pouch. I didn't touch it for outings or clothes.
In January, my spectacles broke. I opened the pouch and got them fixed the same day. No borrowing, no skipped meals. It wasn't much money. It was just enough.

Zainab, you asked on the podcast about the worst planning habit I've seen. Let Afreen tell you about a team I worked on two years ago.
Our lead, a really kind person, padded every estimate. If a task needed two days, she wrote five. If a report needed a week, she wrote three. She said, "Better safe than sorry."
And for a while it felt great. Nobody was stressed. But here's what happened. With five days for a two-day job, people started on day four. Meetings got longer. Emails piled up. Everyone relaxed, because the deadline looked so far away.
Then everything finished on the last possible afternoon anyway, in a rush, with the same late nights as before.
All that extra time never turned into anything saved. It just filled up. By the end of the year, we were slower than the team next door, which padded nothing.

qa.a: If a task needed two days, she wrote five.

qa.a: They probably felt calm and unhurried, since the deadline seemed far away, which is why they started late.

qa.a: They may have seen a team with lots of time on paper that still rushed at the end, and finished slower overall.

Uday, you're adding two extra days to every task on that project plan. Let your Elizabeth Aunty tell you what we learned at the printing press, long before your time.
Everyone on my team padded their tasks. Typesetting, three extra days. Proofreading, two. Binding, four. The plan looked safe. But every task used all its padding, and we were still late.
One year our manager sat us down. She said, "Take the padding out of each task. Give me honest times. Then we'll keep one buffer, ten days, at the very end, before the delivery date. Nobody touches it unless something real goes wrong."
At first we were nervous. Then the big binding machine broke for six days. We took six from the buffer and still delivered on time, with four days left over.
That buffer belonged to everyone, so nobody wasted it.

The school renovation had to be finished before the monsoon, and Pema, the site coordinator, had only nine weeks. Every contractor's estimate came padded: painters wanted three extra days, electricians four, the plumber a week.
Her deputy Rashmi added them up. "With all the padding, we finish two weeks after the rains start."
Pema took a red pen. "Everyone gives me their honest time. No cushions." Then she drew a block at the end of the chart. "Eight days here. Shared. Anyone who hits a real delay asks me, and we take from this."
The painters grumbled. But without their extra days, they started on the Monday instead of drifting in on Wednesday.
In week six, the cement delivery was stuck at a flooded bridge for three days. Pema took three days from the buffer.
The work finished with five buffer days unused, a week before the first heavy rain.

Our team met in the library about the notes-sharing site for the campus. Vijay had a list of twelve features: upload, search, ratings, user profiles, comments, badges, dark mode, a leaderboard...
I asked the question I'd been thinking about all week: what's the smallest version that's actually useful? If someone can upload their notes and someone else can find them, that's the whole point. Everything else is nice but not needed on day one.

In the end we agreed. Launch with upload and search only. Ratings, profiles and the rest go on a "later" list on the whiteboard. Target: live before mid-sems in three weeks.
I feel lighter. Twelve features felt impossible. Two feels doable.

Dear Farida,
You said you always study with music and it helps. I used to say the same. Then I wondered: does it, though? So I tested it on myself.
For one week, I did the same kind of maths sums every evening: twenty from the same chapter, timed. Monday, Wednesday and Friday with my usual music. Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday in silence. Same desk, same time, seven o'clock. I wrote the time taken and the number right in a small table.
Results: with music, I averaged 16 right in 31 minutes. Without music, 18 right in 27 minutes.
It's only one week and only me. But it surprised me. Now I keep music for drawing and silence for maths.
Want to try it too? Same rules: change only the music, keep everything else the same.
Madhav

Leela, you asked on your channel how I found out music was ruining my studying. So here's Ujjwal's little experiment.
I always had songs on while doing physics numericals. I was sure it helped me focus. Then my cousin asked, "How do you know?" And I didn't.
So for two weeks I did an experiment. Every evening, fifteen numericals of the same type, same desk, same time after dinner. One day with music, the next day without. Only one thing changed. I timed myself and wrote the score in a table on the last page of my notebook.
After fourteen days: with music, about eleven right out of fifteen. Without music, about thirteen. And I finished faster in silence, most days.
I'm not saying music is bad for everyone. It was just one person, two weeks. But for me, for physics, silence wins.

qa.q: How many numericals did Ujjwal do each evening?
qa.a: Fifteen numericals of the same type.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel when the cousin asked "How do you know?"
qa.a: Ujjwal felt unsure and a bit caught out, realising the belief that music helped had never been checked.

qa.q: What else could Ujjwal test next using the same method?
qa.a: Ujjwal could test soft instrumental music against songs with words, changing only that one thing, to see if the type of music matters.

qa.q: How might Leela's listeners see Ujjwal's experiment?
qa.a: They may find it simple and useful, and some may try the same test on their own study habits.

grounding: It shows a student changing only whether music plays while doing the same timed sums, and recording the scores in a table to compare.
